paragraphs: I did a two-month clerkship at Lund University in Sweden. I am very happy to have taken part in the overseas study program that I had longed for since before entering university and to have been given valuable experiences. I report here the state of my clerkship life locally and what I learned through studying abroad.

Lund, where I stayed, is located in southern Sweden and is a student town where the city and the university are fused. The grounds of Lund University, which boasts the largest number of students in the Nordic countries, are very wide, and there were many times when, walking through the town, I found myself inside the Lund University campus before I knew it. Although it is Northern Europe, because it is in the south, even in winter the temperature is not too cold, and during March to April, when I stayed, it snowed on only a few days, and it was very comfortable. The official language is Swedish, but most people can speak English, so I had no language difficulty in daily life.

For the first four weeks I did a clerkship in the emergency department of the university hospital in Malmö, the town next to Lund. The emergency department is large, with about 60 doctors enrolled, and a three-shift working system was used: Day shift (8-15), Evening shift (15-22) and Night shift (22 to 8 the next day). At the morning handover about 80 staff including nurses took part, and I was very nervous when I introduced myself in front of everyone on the first day of the clerkship. The clerkship was in a shadowing format, following a different doctor every day. Since examinations and chart writing were in Swedish, the doctor translated into English each time. Because Sweden accepts many immigrants, there were also patients who wished to be examined in English, and in those cases I was entrusted to do history taking, physical examination and even reporting to the senior on my own. I was happy to be able to use, in the clinical setting from the first day, the English physical examination I had practiced in the pre-dispatch training. Thanks to the educationally enthusiastic doctors, who let me think about differential diagnoses from the content of the history and assess, and gave me feedback on my presentations, I was able to spend days full of learning. One of the differences from Japan that I felt in the clerkship is the large discretion of nurses. In Sweden, the first touch of a patient who comes to the emergency department is done by a nurse, who can take the history, decide triage and decide to send home if mild. In addition, the tests to be ordered and the drugs to be prescribed for each symptom are decided in advance, and when a patient fits them, the nurse issues test orders and prescription instructions. Often the necessary blood test results and X-rays were already available before the doctor examined the patient, and I felt it was very efficient for deciding the treatment policy. Also, a known problem of the Swedish healthcare system is the long waiting time until access to medical care. For mild patients, there was often a wait of five to six hours from arrival at the emergency department until seeing a doctor. The parts that are hard to handle immediately because of a doctor shortage were compensated for by task shifting and the spread of a 24-hour public medical consultation dial.

For the last four weeks I did a clerkship in the pediatrics department of a community hospital in a town called Växjö, about two and a half hours by train from Lund. During my stay, Lund University Hospital had no acceptance of pediatrics clerkships, and instead I was told a pediatrics clerkship was possible at a community hospital, so I was able to do my clerkship at Växjö Central Hospital. Since none of my seniors had visited before, I had no prior information and was anxious, but I could also come into contact with common diseases peculiar to a community hospital, and it became a very valuable experience. There were about 20 pediatrics doctors, all very friendly, who always looked out for me during the clerkship to see if I had any trouble, and the atmosphere was homelike. Each week I observed various scenes of pediatric care: the general ward, specialist outpatient clinics, the emergency outpatient department and the NICU. In the outpatient observation week I was allowed to observe specialist clinics such as cardiology, allergy and rheumatology. The number of patients one doctor takes is small, 8 to 10 a day, and I was impressed that they took a long 40 to 60 minutes per person, listening to each patient thoroughly and examining them carefully. In the emergency outpatient department, I was impressed by the high convenience of the chart system linked to the My Number system. In Swedish hospitals a common chart is used for each region, so even when emergency care is provided on referral from a family doctor, the patient's medical information such as history, visit history and medication history can be grasped at a glance on the same chart, and responses were very efficient. What shocked me most was the difference in the NICU. In Japanese NICUs it is common for newborn beds to be lined up in a large room so that doctors and nurses can monitor them in case of sudden changes. In Sweden, on the other hand, the concept of family-centered care, so that babies can spend as much time as possible with their families, has permeated, and the NICU is managed with all rooms private, with an adult bed next to the incubator where the parents can stay overnight. Sweden has a well-developed parental leave system, and the rate of fathers taking parental leave exceeds 90%, and it was also very impressive that in most rooms both parents were staying over to care for the baby. I felt it was how a NICU should be, staying close to the feelings of the baby and family. Introducing it immediately is difficult because of the number of medical staff, facilities and space, but I want to think about what I can do to bring it to Japan.

Sweden is known as an advanced country in gender equality, and women's advancement in society is progressing, with female doctors making up 90% in the pediatrics department where I did my clerkship, and the gender ratio of Lund University medical students in recent years being more women. A work-life balance is in place, and because housework, childbirth and child rearing are not seen as belonging only to women, I felt great appeal in that it is easier for female doctors to continue their careers. I felt that the spirit of fairness is rooted not only between men and women but in society as a whole. For example, in Sweden doctors, nurses and medical staff call each other by first name without honorifics. Even professors are called without Dr. or Prof., and I found the flat relationships very fresh. In Sweden there is a coffee break culture called Fika, and many schools and offices set aside Fika time. Within the hospital too, they gave handovers with coffee in hand and sweets, and made coffee between tasks to take a breather and enjoy communication among medical staff, working with leeway in their hearts. Also, everyone values time with their family, and few overtime hours and long vacations are characteristics of the way of working. I was greatly shocked that not a single doctor works overtime after 17:00 and that even doctors can take a summer vacation of four to six weeks.

In this study abroad I gained a great deal of learning not only from medical settings but also from differences in social systems, culture and lifestyle. While valuing the stimulation I received this time, I would like to maintain high motivation in my residency life after graduation and work even harder. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office, the doctors and students of Lund University, and everyone who supported this study abroad, who gave me this valuable opportunity for study abroad.
